summary: Captures the background and thinking from the LEMONADE working group, which was chartered to enhance Internet mail for diverse clients, such as mobile handhelds on limited links. It discusses needed protocol enhancements and design principles, with backward compatibility. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A history of why people wanted email to work better on small phones and slow connections, while still working with old email systems.

questions: what was the lemonade working group
subtitle: Design principles for mobile email across phones, networks, and media types

tldr.problem: Mobile devices have limited power, memory, and bandwidth, and wireless links are unreliable and expensive. Standard Internet email protocols were designed for desktop computers and wired networks, making them poorly suited to mobile phones.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC documents requirements from the LEMONADE working group for protocol enhancements to support mobile clients, including thin voice clients, text-based phone interfaces, and graphical devices, while maintaining backward compatibility with existing email systems.
tldr.outcome: The documented requirements and principles guided development of IMAP extensions and other protocol work to make Internet email practical on mobile handsets and to unify email with voice and fax messaging.

today: RFC 4416 is an Internet Standard. It successfully guided the development of IMAP extensions and email protocols for mobile devices. Modern smartphones routinely receive email via enhanced IMAP with push notifications, demonstrating how the RFC's requirements shaped real-world email systems.

sections.title: The Mobile Email Challenge
sections.content:
The LEMONADE working group (Internet email to support diverse service environments) was chartered to enhance Internet mail protocols so they could work effectively on mobile devices. Historically, email, voice mail, fax, and SMS evolved as separate systems using different protocols and networks. LEMONADE's goal was to enable a unified infrastructure where a single protocol and mailbox could serve all message types on all devices.

Mobile devices present unique challenges: they have less processing power and memory than desktops; wireless networks offer lower bandwidth, higher latency, and less reliability; users are charged by the amount of data transferred; and devices may lose network connectivity temporarily. Additionally, devices must support voice-based interfaces (for phones), text-only interfaces (for older devices), and full graphical interfaces (for modern smartphones). The RFC documents the requirements that emerged from considering these constraints.
sections.plainLanguage: Phones are much weaker than computers: slower processors, less memory, expensive slow wireless. Email system needs to be redesigned to work with these limits instead of ignoring them.

sections.title: Messaging Models and Client Profiles
sections.content:
The RFC identifies three primary client profiles for mobile email:

TUI (Telephone User Interface) clients use voice or simple telephone keypads to interact with email. A typical TUI client announces "you have two new voice messages, six unheard emails, and one new fax", then allows the user to navigate and play back messages using touch tones. TUI clients need access to mailbox summaries without downloading every message header.

WUI (Wireless User Interface) clients run on handheld devices like phones and PDAs with small screens and limited input. They need to minimize data transfer due to bandwidth constraints and cost. Users want to download message headers and select which content to retrieve, avoiding unnecessary downloads of large attachments.

Multi-modal clients combine TUI and WUI functionality, allowing users to access the same mailbox through both voice and visual interfaces simultaneously. A single message might be checked via voice while also viewing headers on a screen.

All three models must work with existing email infrastructure and accommodate voice messages, faxes, and text emails in a unified system.
sections.plainLanguage: Phone email comes in three styles: voice-only (you listen to email), tiny screen with keyboard (you read and type), or both at once. All three need to work with the same mailbox.

sections.title: Message Retrieval Protocol Requirements
sections.content:
The RFC documents requirements for IMAP (Internet Message Access Protocol), the standard for rich message retrieval. For mobile devices, IMAP needs several enhancements:

Performance issues include real-time playback of voice messages (voice is extremely sensitive to latency and must begin playing within seconds), and avoiding content-transfer-encoding inflation where binary data like audio is expanded 30% when encoded as text.

Functional issues include mailbox summary support (showing counts of new messages by type without downloading headers), sort support by message context (presenting voice messages first, then faxes), and status of multiple mailboxes (checking sub-mailboxes efficiently without logging into each one). Clients also need access to specialized mailboxes like Inbox, Sent Items, and Deleted Items with standardized naming.

Additional requirements address simultaneous logins (important when both a voice client and a web client access the same mailbox), and support for restrictions on sensitive information like caller ID.
sections.plainLanguage: IMAP needs to be faster and smarter for phones: play voice messages immediately, show message counts without downloading everything, and let you check all your folders without logging in multiple times.

sections.title: Message Submission and Notification
sections.content:
The RFC identifies requirements for sending messages and notifying users of new mail:

Submission challenges include forwarding large messages without downloading them entirely (a mobile user might want to forward a video attachment without downloading it first), quota enforcement per message context (so voice messages don't fill the mailbox preventing email delivery), and support for scheduled delivery with cancellation (allowing users to queue messages for sending later).

Notification is critical for mobile devices because polling for new messages constantly drains batteries and uses expensive bandwidth. Mobile messaging systems like SMS and MMS use server-to-client push notification, but Internet email had no standardized notification protocol. The RFC documents requirements for a notification mechanism that allows servers to push notifications to clients about new messages, message read events, and mailbox conditions.

For multimodal clients, synchronization between different interfaces is needed so that if a message is read via voice interface, the visual interface updates to show it as read.
sections.plainLanguage: You need to send messages without downloading giant attachments, limit each message type so one doesn't clog everything, and get instant notifications when new mail arrives instead of constantly asking the server.

sections.title: Wireless Network and Device Constraints
sections.content:
The RFC details the practical constraints of wireless mobile devices:

Transport issues include frequent connection interruptions due to signal loss, handoffs between cell towers, incoming voice calls interrupting data sessions, and IP address changes during a session. The mobile protocol must recover gracefully from these interruptions.

Device limitations include small memory, slow processors, limited storage, small displays showing only a few lines of text, and minimal input capabilities (a phone keypad rather than a full keyboard).

Bandwidth issues mean users are sensitive to data costs and want to download only what they need. Email clients that automatically download entire messages with large attachments are unsuitable. Additionally, many file formats that desktop clients support (like PDF, Microsoft Office documents) are not useful on phones, making content adaptation desirable.

Display considerations include limited screen size and color depth, inability to display multiple images simultaneously, and need for media transcoding so that an image optimized for desktop display is resized and recompressed for phone display.
sections.plainLanguage: Phones lose signal constantly, have tiny screens, slow brains, and expensive data. Email needs to cope with all of that: reconnect automatically, show just enough to read, and shrink big files to fit small screens.

sections.title: Guiding Design Principles
sections.content:
The RFC documents five principles to guide protocol enhancements:

Protocol conservation: Reuse existing protocols and don't redefine their semantics. Backward compatibility is mandatory—messages created with enhanced clients must be usable by old clients, even if with reduced functionality.

Sensible reception and sending context: When a sender marks a message as a voice message, voice message semantics should apply at the receiving end. When a user sends, they should be able to specify the message context (voice, text, fax, video).

Internet infrastructure preservation: The existing email infrastructure must continue working. Extensions are added only where required, and all enhancements must be backward compatible.

Voice requirements: Voice messages need near-real-time delivery with minimal latency variation, since voice is sensitive to playback delay.

Video requirements: The framework must scale for very large messages, with streaming support in both directions.
sections.plainLanguage: Five principles guide the work: reuse old protocols, preserve all their capabilities, let senders say what type of message they're sending, don't break email infrastructure, and handle real-time voice and huge videos.
